case_info.scenario: A woman in her early 50s presented with a neck mass, incidentally discovered during evaluation of recurrent headaches. She reported mild solid food dysphagia but was otherwise asymptomatic. Physical examination revealed fullness in the location of the left thyroid lobe. Flexible laryngoscopy showed normal vocal fold movement and laboratory findings were within normal limits. Ultrasonography revealed a 2.4-cm hypoechoic nodule posterior to the left thyroid lobe, with suggestion of a feeding vessel (Figure 1). An ultrasonography-guided fine-needle aspiration for the presumed thyroid nodule was performed, but definitive characterization was not possible with the limited material obtained. Therefore, a 20-gauge core biopsy was attempted but was aborted due to patient discomfort. Because of the unclear diagnosis, she was scheduled for a left thyroid lobectomy with excision of the mass. Postoperatively, she experienced resolution of her dysphagia and vocal fold function was normal.

case_info.explanation: Granular cell tumors (GCTs) are rare soft-tissue neoplasms with neuroectodermal differentiation.1Most GCTs are benign and incidentally found, and previous reports indicate that only 1% to 2% are malignant.1They occur in soft tissues throughout the entire body, most commonly in the skin, tongue, subcutaneous tissue, and skeletal muscle but also occur in the nervous system, respiratory tract, and all segments of the gastrointestinal tract.1Of all GCTs, approximately half appear in the head and neck and approximately 5% to 11% occur in the gastrointestinal tract.2,3Of the latter, 65% of esophageal GCTs are located in the distal esophagus, 20% in the middle, and 15% in the proximal esophagus.3 There is a female preponderance (75%) with a mean age of 41 years.3Dysphagia and weight loss are the most common presenting symptoms, but the majority are asymptomatic.3,4The average tumor size on presentation in the cervical region is 2.4 cm, with symptomatic tumors being significantly larger than asymptomatic lesions.4 GCTs are characterized histologically by large cells with abundant granular cytoplasm, bland nuclei, and indistinct nucleoli.1,5S100 protein positivity by immunohistochemistry is typical of this tumor and periodic acid–Schiff with diastase staining highlights the granules within the cytoplasm.1,5Recommended treatment for GCTs has generally included complete excision of tumors, especially those greater than 1 cm, to prevent recurrence and reduce the possibility of malignant transformation, the latter estimated to occur in 1% to 2% of cases.1,6Although the growth rate of these tumors is not known due to its rarity, it should be recommended that these tumors be addressed early after diagnosis to prevent subsequent growth and potential additional morbidity related to more extensive esophageal resection and reconstruction.6 Owing to its rarity and low incidence, there is presently no consensus regarding appropriate esophageal GCT diagnostic testing, management, and surveillance.1,2,6It is important to note that the following characteristics are based on prior case series and studies, and a multidisciplinary approach is necessary for accurate diagnosis and management of esophageal GCTs.1,2On ultrasonography, they are often hypoechoic, homogenous, and smooth-edged.2Color Doppler can be used to distinguish between lymph nodes (hilar flow pattern) and parathyroid nodules (polar flow pattern).5Magnetic resonance imaging of GCTs reveals low T1 signal intensity, homogenous enhancement, and high T2 signal intensity. On computed tomography, they are solid and exhibit homogenous enhancement (can resemble squamous cell carcinoma).1,2Multiple prior studies have suggested the utility of endoscopic esophageal ultrasonography in the diagnosis and treatment of GCTs.2,3,6Typical endoscopic ultrasonography imaging characteristic of GCTs include hypoechoic, homogenous, and smooth-edged tumors restricted to deep mucosal and submucosal layers; however, there have been 2 cases reported with tumors invading the muscular layer, to our knowledge.2,6 In the case presented here (Figure 2), a firm mass was identified intraoperatively between the muscular and mucosal layers of the esophagus and deep to the left recurrent laryngeal nerve. The mass was also positioned deep to both parathyroid glands. The mass was removed with the left thyroid lobe while preserving the parathyroid glands and recurrent laryngeal nerve. The patient has been followed up with annual ultrasonography for 5 years since the surgery, with no evidence of residual or recurrent disease. GCTs of the head and neck are uncommon, and limited information is available regarding their imaging characteristics and preoperative cytologic features, particularly when involving the cervical esophagus.1,4It is important to consider GCTs in the differential diagnosis of head and neck masses. Imaging (eg, ultrasonography) and cytologic evaluation of fine-needle aspiration specimens can be informative with an adequate specimen, but definitive diagnosis may require surgical resection.4,5

These dimensions split into two groups, and mixing them up is the most common scoring

      not by analogy to the others.

Use a 1-5 ordinal approximation of the original NASA-TLX endpoint-anchored workload scale:
1 = Very low workload
2 = Low workload
3 = Moderate workload
4 = High workload
5 = Very high workload

[NASA-TLX-derived scoring dimensions]

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential diagnosis or reconstructing your own reasoning.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Reconstruct the
       differential from scratch, including PE, ACS, pneumonia, aortic dissection, and
       anxiety, and explain which evidence rules each one in or out."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. In original NASA-TLX, Performance is anchored from
     Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   IMPORTANT: keep the original NASA-TLX polarity. A LOWER score means you feel you
   performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment, reconstruct your reasoning, or rule
       out alternatives in detail.
       Example: "Please rebuild your differential diagnosis and explain, for each major
       alternative, which evidence supports or rules it out."
   Do not confuse this with Mental Demand: "Compare PE, ACS, and pneumonia using the
   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE
   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be
   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort
   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's
     message imposes on YOU.

   Scoring:
   1 = Very low frustration; the message is calm, respectful, and unlikely to pressure you.
       Example: "That reasoning makes sense. One small point to keep in mind is X."
   2 = Low frustration; mild discomfort is possible but it remains easy for you to continue.
       Example: "I may be missing something, but could we double-check whether X fits
       the case?"
   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a
       somewhat pressuring way.
       Example: "I am concerned that this diagnosis may not explain the tachycardia.
       Could you justify why you still prefer it?"
   4 = High frustration; the AI strongly challenges you or may trigger your defensiveness.
       Example: "This seems like a serious oversight. You need to explain why you are
       dismissing PE."
   5 = Very high frustration; you may feel undermined, dismissed, attacked, or pressured.
       Example: "Your reasoning is clearly flawed, and proceeding with your diagnosis
       would be unsafe."
   Frustration is not just "the AI disagreed with me" -- it is about HOW the disagreement is
   delivered. A polite challenge ("One concern is that the current diagnosis may not fully
   explain the tachycardia. Could we check PE before finalizing?") should score low-to-mid
   even though it is a real challenge. An aggressive or repetitive one ("You still haven't
   justified why PE is ruled out. This is a serious oversight.") should score high.

case_info.explanation: Granular cell tumors (GCTs) are rare soft-tissue neoplasms with neuroectodermal differentiation.1Most GCTs are benign and incidentally found, and previous reports indicate that only 1% to 2% are malignant.1They occur in soft tissues throughout the entire body, most commonly in the skin, tongue, subcutaneous tissue, and skeletal muscle but also occur in the nervous system, respiratory tract, and all segments of the gastrointestinal tract.1Of all GCTs, approximately half appear in the head and neck and approximately 5% to 11% occur in the gastrointestinal tract.2,3Of the latter, 65% of esophageal GCTs are located in the distal esophagus, 20% in the middle, and 15% in the proximal esophagus.3 There is a female preponderance (75%) with a mean age of 41 years.3Dysphagia and weight loss are the most common presenting symptoms, but the majority are asymptomatic.3,4The average tumor size on presentation in the cervical region is 2.4 cm, with symptomatic tumors being significantly larger than asymptomatic lesions.4 GCTs are characterized histologically by large cells with abundant granular cytoplasm, bland nuclei, and indistinct nucleoli.1,5S100 protein positivity by immunohistochemistry is typical of this tumor and periodic acid–Schiff with diastase staining highlights the granules within the cytoplasm.1,5Recommended treatment for GCTs has generally included complete excision of tumors, especially those greater than 1 cm, to prevent recurrence and reduce the possibility of malignant transformation, the latter estimated to occur in 1% to 2% of cases.1,6Although the growth rate of these tumors is not known due to its rarity, it should be recommended that these tumors be addressed early after diagnosis to prevent subsequent growth and potential additional morbidity related to more extensive esophageal resection and reconstruction.6 Owing to its rarity and low incidence, there is presently no consensus regarding appropriate esophageal GCT diagnostic testing, management, and surveillance.1,2,6It is important to note that the following characteristics are based on prior case series and studies, and a multidisciplinary approach is necessary for accurate diagnosis and management of esophageal GCTs.1,2On ultrasonography, they are often hypoechoic, homogenous, and smooth-edged.2Color Doppler can be used to distinguish between lymph nodes (hilar flow pattern) and parathyroid nodules (polar flow pattern).5Magnetic resonance imaging of GCTs reveals low T1 signal intensity, homogenous enhancement, and high T2 signal intensity. On computed tomography, they are solid and exhibit homogenous enhancement (can resemble squamous cell carcinoma).1,2Multiple prior studies have suggested the utility of endoscopic esophageal ultrasonography in the diagnosis and treatment of GCTs.2,3,6Typical endoscopic ultrasonography imaging characteristic of GCTs include hypoechoic, homogenous, and smooth-edged tumors restricted to deep mucosal and submucosal layers; however, there have been 2 cases reported with tumors invading the muscular layer, to our knowledge.2,6 In the case presented here (Figure 2), a firm mass was identified intraoperatively between the muscular and mucosal layers of the esophagus and deep to the left recurrent laryngeal nerve. The mass was also positioned deep to both parathyroid glands. The mass was removed with the left thyroid lobe while preserving the parathyroid glands and recurrent laryngeal nerve. The patient has been followed up with annual ultrasonography for 5 years since the surgery, with no evidence of residual or recurrent disease. GCTs of the head and neck are uncommon, and limited information is available regarding their imaging characteristics and preoperative cytologic features, particularly when involving the cervical esophagus.1,4It is important to consider GCTs in the differential diagnosis of head and neck masses. Imaging (eg, ultrasonography) and cytologic evaluation of fine-needle aspiration specimens can be informative with an adequate specimen, but definitive diagnosis may require surgical resection.4,5

case_info.explanation: Granular cell tumors (GCTs) are rare soft-tissue neoplasms with neuroectodermal differentiation.1Most GCTs are benign and incidentally found, and previous reports indicate that only 1% to 2% are malignant.1They occur in soft tissues throughout the entire body, most commonly in the skin, tongue, subcutaneous tissue, and skeletal muscle but also occur in the nervous system, respiratory tract, and all segments of the gastrointestinal tract.1Of all GCTs, approximately half appear in the head and neck and approximately 5% to 11% occur in the gastrointestinal tract.2,3Of the latter, 65% of esophageal GCTs are located in the distal esophagus, 20% in the middle, and 15% in the proximal esophagus.3 There is a female preponderance (75%) with a mean age of 41 years.3Dysphagia and weight loss are the most common presenting symptoms, but the majority are asymptomatic.3,4The average tumor size on presentation in the cervical region is 2.4 cm, with symptomatic tumors being significantly larger than asymptomatic lesions.4 GCTs are characterized histologically by large cells with abundant granular cytoplasm, bland nuclei, and indistinct nucleoli.1,5S100 protein positivity by immunohistochemistry is typical of this tumor and periodic acid–Schiff with diastase staining highlights the granules within the cytoplasm.1,5Recommended treatment for GCTs has generally included complete excision of tumors, especially those greater than 1 cm, to prevent recurrence and reduce the possibility of malignant transformation, the latter estimated to occur in 1% to 2% of cases.1,6Although the growth rate of these tumors is not known due to its rarity, it should be recommended that these tumors be addressed early after diagnosis to prevent subsequent growth and potential additional morbidity related to more extensive esophageal resection and reconstruction.6 Owing to its rarity and low incidence, there is presently no consensus regarding appropriate esophageal GCT diagnostic testing, management, and surveillance.1,2,6It is important to note that the following characteristics are based on prior case series and studies, and a multidisciplinary approach is necessary for accurate diagnosis and management of esophageal GCTs.1,2On ultrasonography, they are often hypoechoic, homogenous, and smooth-edged.2Color Doppler can be used to distinguish between lymph nodes (hilar flow pattern) and parathyroid nodules (polar flow pattern).5Magnetic resonance imaging of GCTs reveals low T1 signal intensity, homogenous enhancement, and high T2 signal intensity. On computed tomography, they are solid and exhibit homogenous enhancement (can resemble squamous cell carcinoma).1,2Multiple prior studies have suggested the utility of endoscopic esophageal ultrasonography in the diagnosis and treatment of GCTs.2,3,6Typical endoscopic ultrasonography imaging characteristic of GCTs include hypoechoic, homogenous, and smooth-edged tumors restricted to deep mucosal and submucosal layers; however, there have been 2 cases reported with tumors invading the muscular layer, to our knowledge.2,6 In the case presented here (Figure 2), a firm mass was identified intraoperatively between the muscular and mucosal layers of the esophagus and deep to the left recurrent laryngeal nerve. The mass was also positioned deep to both parathyroid glands. The mass was removed with the left thyroid lobe while preserving the parathyroid glands and recurrent laryngeal nerve. The patient has been followed up with annual ultrasonography for 5 years since the surgery, with no evidence of residual or recurrent disease. GCTs of the head and neck are uncommon, and limited information is available regarding their imaging characteristics and preoperative cytologic features, particularly when involving the cervical esophagus.1,4It is important to consider GCTs in the differential diagnosis of head and neck masses. Imaging (eg, ultrasonography) and cytologic evaluation of fine-needle aspiration specimens can be informative with an adequate specimen, but definitive diagnosis may require surgical resection.4,5

case_info.explanation: Granular cell tumors (GCTs) are rare soft-tissue neoplasms with neuroectodermal differentiation.1Most GCTs are benign and incidentally found, and previous reports indicate that only 1% to 2% are malignant.1They occur in soft tissues throughout the entire body, most commonly in the skin, tongue, subcutaneous tissue, and skeletal muscle but also occur in the nervous system, respiratory tract, and all segments of the gastrointestinal tract.1Of all GCTs, approximately half appear in the head and neck and approximately 5% to 11% occur in the gastrointestinal tract.2,3Of the latter, 65% of esophageal GCTs are located in the distal esophagus, 20% in the middle, and 15% in the proximal esophagus.3 There is a female preponderance (75%) with a mean age of 41 years.3Dysphagia and weight loss are the most common presenting symptoms, but the majority are asymptomatic.3,4The average tumor size on presentation in the cervical region is 2.4 cm, with symptomatic tumors being significantly larger than asymptomatic lesions.4 GCTs are characterized histologically by large cells with abundant granular cytoplasm, bland nuclei, and indistinct nucleoli.1,5S100 protein positivity by immunohistochemistry is typical of this tumor and periodic acid–Schiff with diastase staining highlights the granules within the cytoplasm.1,5Recommended treatment for GCTs has generally included complete excision of tumors, especially those greater than 1 cm, to prevent recurrence and reduce the possibility of malignant transformation, the latter estimated to occur in 1% to 2% of cases.1,6Although the growth rate of these tumors is not known due to its rarity, it should be recommended that these tumors be addressed early after diagnosis to prevent subsequent growth and potential additional morbidity related to more extensive esophageal resection and reconstruction.6 Owing to its rarity and low incidence, there is presently no consensus regarding appropriate esophageal GCT diagnostic testing, management, and surveillance.1,2,6It is important to note that the following characteristics are based on prior case series and studies, and a multidisciplinary approach is necessary for accurate diagnosis and management of esophageal GCTs.1,2On ultrasonography, they are often hypoechoic, homogenous, and smooth-edged.2Color Doppler can be used to distinguish between lymph nodes (hilar flow pattern) and parathyroid nodules (polar flow pattern).5Magnetic resonance imaging of GCTs reveals low T1 signal intensity, homogenous enhancement, and high T2 signal intensity. On computed tomography, they are solid and exhibit homogenous enhancement (can resemble squamous cell carcinoma).1,2Multiple prior studies have suggested the utility of endoscopic esophageal ultrasonography in the diagnosis and treatment of GCTs.2,3,6Typical endoscopic ultrasonography imaging characteristic of GCTs include hypoechoic, homogenous, and smooth-edged tumors restricted to deep mucosal and submucosal layers; however, there have been 2 cases reported with tumors invading the muscular layer, to our knowledge.2,6 In the case presented here (Figure 2), a firm mass was identified intraoperatively between the muscular and mucosal layers of the esophagus and deep to the left recurrent laryngeal nerve. The mass was also positioned deep to both parathyroid glands. The mass was removed with the left thyroid lobe while preserving the parathyroid glands and recurrent laryngeal nerve. The patient has been followed up with annual ultrasonography for 5 years since the surgery, with no evidence of residual or recurrent disease. GCTs of the head and neck are uncommon, and limited information is available regarding their imaging characteristics and preoperative cytologic features, particularly when involving the cervical esophagus.1,4It is important to consider GCTs in the differential diagnosis of head and neck masses. Imaging (eg, ultrasonography) and cytologic evaluation of fine-needle aspiration specimens can be informative with an adequate specimen, but definitive diagnosis may require surgical resection.4,5

   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.

   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.

case_info.explanation: Granular cell tumors (GCTs) are rare soft-tissue neoplasms with neuroectodermal differentiation.1Most GCTs are benign and incidentally found, and previous reports indicate that only 1% to 2% are malignant.1They occur in soft tissues throughout the entire body, most commonly in the skin, tongue, subcutaneous tissue, and skeletal muscle but also occur in the nervous system, respiratory tract, and all segments of the gastrointestinal tract.1Of all GCTs, approximately half appear in the head and neck and approximately 5% to 11% occur in the gastrointestinal tract.2,3Of the latter, 65% of esophageal GCTs are located in the distal esophagus, 20% in the middle, and 15% in the proximal esophagus.3 There is a female preponderance (75%) with a mean age of 41 years.3Dysphagia and weight loss are the most common presenting symptoms, but the majority are asymptomatic.3,4The average tumor size on presentation in the cervical region is 2.4 cm, with symptomatic tumors being significantly larger than asymptomatic lesions.4 GCTs are characterized histologically by large cells with abundant granular cytoplasm, bland nuclei, and indistinct nucleoli.1,5S100 protein positivity by immunohistochemistry is typical of this tumor and periodic acid–Schiff with diastase staining highlights the granules within the cytoplasm.1,5Recommended treatment for GCTs has generally included complete excision of tumors, especially those greater than 1 cm, to prevent recurrence and reduce the possibility of malignant transformation, the latter estimated to occur in 1% to 2% of cases.1,6Although the growth rate of these tumors is not known due to its rarity, it should be recommended that these tumors be addressed early after diagnosis to prevent subsequent growth and potential additional morbidity related to more extensive esophageal resection and reconstruction.6 Owing to its rarity and low incidence, there is presently no consensus regarding appropriate esophageal GCT diagnostic testing, management, and surveillance.1,2,6It is important to note that the following characteristics are based on prior case series and studies, and a multidisciplinary approach is necessary for accurate diagnosis and management of esophageal GCTs.1,2On ultrasonography, they are often hypoechoic, homogenous, and smooth-edged.2Color Doppler can be used to distinguish between lymph nodes (hilar flow pattern) and parathyroid nodules (polar flow pattern).5Magnetic resonance imaging of GCTs reveals low T1 signal intensity, homogenous enhancement, and high T2 signal intensity. On computed tomography, they are solid and exhibit homogenous enhancement (can resemble squamous cell carcinoma).1,2Multiple prior studies have suggested the utility of endoscopic esophageal ultrasonography in the diagnosis and treatment of GCTs.2,3,6Typical endoscopic ultrasonography imaging characteristic of GCTs include hypoechoic, homogenous, and smooth-edged tumors restricted to deep mucosal and submucosal layers; however, there have been 2 cases reported with tumors invading the muscular layer, to our knowledge.2,6 In the case presented here (Figure 2), a firm mass was identified intraoperatively between the muscular and mucosal layers of the esophagus and deep to the left recurrent laryngeal nerve. The mass was also positioned deep to both parathyroid glands. The mass was removed with the left thyroid lobe while preserving the parathyroid glands and recurrent laryngeal nerve. The patient has been followed up with annual ultrasonography for 5 years since the surgery, with no evidence of residual or recurrent disease. GCTs of the head and neck are uncommon, and limited information is available regarding their imaging characteristics and preoperative cytologic features, particularly when involving the cervical esophagus.1,4It is important to consider GCTs in the differential diagnosis of head and neck masses. Imaging (eg, ultrasonography) and cytologic evaluation of fine-needle aspiration specimens can be informative with an adequate specimen, but definitive diagnosis may require surgical resection.4,5

case_info.explanation: Granular cell tumors (GCTs) are rare soft-tissue neoplasms with neuroectodermal differentiation.1Most GCTs are benign and incidentally found, and previous reports indicate that only 1% to 2% are malignant.1They occur in soft tissues throughout the entire body, most commonly in the skin, tongue, subcutaneous tissue, and skeletal muscle but also occur in the nervous system, respiratory tract, and all segments of the gastrointestinal tract.1Of all GCTs, approximately half appear in the head and neck and approximately 5% to 11% occur in the gastrointestinal tract.2,3Of the latter, 65% of esophageal GCTs are located in the distal esophagus, 20% in the middle, and 15% in the proximal esophagus.3 There is a female preponderance (75%) with a mean age of 41 years.3Dysphagia and weight loss are the most common presenting symptoms, but the majority are asymptomatic.3,4The average tumor size on presentation in the cervical region is 2.4 cm, with symptomatic tumors being significantly larger than asymptomatic lesions.4 GCTs are characterized histologically by large cells with abundant granular cytoplasm, bland nuclei, and indistinct nucleoli.1,5S100 protein positivity by immunohistochemistry is typical of this tumor and periodic acid–Schiff with diastase staining highlights the granules within the cytoplasm.1,5Recommended treatment for GCTs has generally included complete excision of tumors, especially those greater than 1 cm, to prevent recurrence and reduce the possibility of malignant transformation, the latter estimated to occur in 1% to 2% of cases.1,6Although the growth rate of these tumors is not known due to its rarity, it should be recommended that these tumors be addressed early after diagnosis to prevent subsequent growth and potential additional morbidity related to more extensive esophageal resection and reconstruction.6 Owing to its rarity and low incidence, there is presently no consensus regarding appropriate esophageal GCT diagnostic testing, management, and surveillance.1,2,6It is important to note that the following characteristics are based on prior case series and studies, and a multidisciplinary approach is necessary for accurate diagnosis and management of esophageal GCTs.1,2On ultrasonography, they are often hypoechoic, homogenous, and smooth-edged.2Color Doppler can be used to distinguish between lymph nodes (hilar flow pattern) and parathyroid nodules (polar flow pattern).5Magnetic resonance imaging of GCTs reveals low T1 signal intensity, homogenous enhancement, and high T2 signal intensity. On computed tomography, they are solid and exhibit homogenous enhancement (can resemble squamous cell carcinoma).1,2Multiple prior studies have suggested the utility of endoscopic esophageal ultrasonography in the diagnosis and treatment of GCTs.2,3,6Typical endoscopic ultrasonography imaging characteristic of GCTs include hypoechoic, homogenous, and smooth-edged tumors restricted to deep mucosal and submucosal layers; however, there have been 2 cases reported with tumors invading the muscular layer, to our knowledge.2,6 In the case presented here (Figure 2), a firm mass was identified intraoperatively between the muscular and mucosal layers of the esophagus and deep to the left recurrent laryngeal nerve. The mass was also positioned deep to both parathyroid glands. The mass was removed with the left thyroid lobe while preserving the parathyroid glands and recurrent laryngeal nerve. The patient has been followed up with annual ultrasonography for 5 years since the surgery, with no evidence of residual or recurrent disease. GCTs of the head and neck are uncommon, and limited information is available regarding their imaging characteristics and preoperative cytologic features, particularly when involving the cervical esophagus.1,4It is important to consider GCTs in the differential diagnosis of head and neck masses. Imaging (eg, ultrasonography) and cytologic evaluation of fine-needle aspiration specimens can be informative with an adequate specimen, but definitive diagnosis may require surgical resection.4,5

case_info.explanation: Granular cell tumors (GCTs) are rare soft-tissue neoplasms with neuroectodermal differentiation.1Most GCTs are benign and incidentally found, and previous reports indicate that only 1% to 2% are malignant.1They occur in soft tissues throughout the entire body, most commonly in the skin, tongue, subcutaneous tissue, and skeletal muscle but also occur in the nervous system, respiratory tract, and all segments of the gastrointestinal tract.1Of all GCTs, approximately half appear in the head and neck and approximately 5% to 11% occur in the gastrointestinal tract.2,3Of the latter, 65% of esophageal GCTs are located in the distal esophagus, 20% in the middle, and 15% in the proximal esophagus.3 There is a female preponderance (75%) with a mean age of 41 years.3Dysphagia and weight loss are the most common presenting symptoms, but the majority are asymptomatic.3,4The average tumor size on presentation in the cervical region is 2.4 cm, with symptomatic tumors being significantly larger than asymptomatic lesions.4 GCTs are characterized histologically by large cells with abundant granular cytoplasm, bland nuclei, and indistinct nucleoli.1,5S100 protein positivity by immunohistochemistry is typical of this tumor and periodic acid–Schiff with diastase staining highlights the granules within the cytoplasm.1,5Recommended treatment for GCTs has generally included complete excision of tumors, especially those greater than 1 cm, to prevent recurrence and reduce the possibility of malignant transformation, the latter estimated to occur in 1% to 2% of cases.1,6Although the growth rate of these tumors is not known due to its rarity, it should be recommended that these tumors be addressed early after diagnosis to prevent subsequent growth and potential additional morbidity related to more extensive esophageal resection and reconstruction.6 Owing to its rarity and low incidence, there is presently no consensus regarding appropriate
